analysis.one_liner: Bars employers and health insurers from using people's genetic information against them.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a Republican senator with 45 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill cleared committee in two months and was signed into law by President Bush in May 2008.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it illegal for health insurers — group plans, individual-market plans, and Medicare supplemental (Medigap) policies — to deny coverage, set premiums, or require genetic tests based on a person's genetic information or their use of genetic services. It makes it illegal for employers, employment agencies, and unions to hire, fire, classify, or train people based on genetic information, and it bars them from demanding employees' genetic information or family medical history, with narrow exceptions such as voluntary wellness programs and legally required workplace toxics monitoring. Genetic information must be kept in separate confidential medical files, and violations carry civil penalties and, in some cases, retroactive reinstatement of coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a family history of genetic disease — people carrying gene variants like BRCA mutations, for example — who previously risked losing health coverage or a job if a test result surfaced. It also protects workers whose genetic information their employer happens to obtain, and it protects people who want to take advantage of genetic testing or counseling without fear that the result will follow them into an insurance office or a hiring interview.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans, individual-market insurers, and Medigap issuers from denying or conditioning coverage or adjusting premiums on the basis of genetic information, including a request for or receipt of genetic services.
Bars health insurers from requesting or requiring an individual or family member to undergo a genetic test.

Makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer, employment agency, labor organization, or training program to discriminate, segregate, or classify based on genetic information, and bars them from requesting, requiring, or purchasing employees' genetic information outside narrow exceptions.
Requires genetic information held by employers to be kept on separate forms in confidential medical files, with strict limits on disclosure.

Extends federal medical-privacy rules to genetic information and bars insurers from using or buying genetic information for underwriting, rating, or enrollment decisions, with penalty authority for violations.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers lose the ability to price or deny coverage using genetic risk, spreading that cost across all enrollees instead of onto the people with the genetic risk. Employers and unions take on compliance work — separating and safeguarding genetic records and policing what they may ask — and lose the option of genetic screening in hiring.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers health insurance and employment only. It leaves life insurance, disability insurance, and long-term care insurance free to deny or price policies using genetic test results — a gap people at genetic risk still face when buying those products.

Insurers may still charge based on conditions that have already manifested. The bill's definitions exclude manifest disease from 'genetic information,' so protection stops at the point a genetic risk becomes a diagnosed illness.

The bill explicitly provides that disparate impact does not create a legal claim, and instead creates a study commission to advise Congress years later on whether to add one — so practices that fall more heavily on particular groups are harder to challenge.

The wellness-program exception lets employers offer genetic services and collect genetic information with an employee's written, voluntary authorization, a carve-out privacy advocates have flagged as a channel for pressure on workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are broad and enforceable, with civil penalties, retroactive reinstatement of wrongly denied coverage, and coordinated enforcement across three cabinet departments. The compliance burden on insurers and employers is real but modest. The honest limitation is scope: the biggest residual risk for people who learn their genetic risk is in life, disability, and long-term care insurance, which this law does not touch.

outcome.mechanism: It moved fast — referred to the Senate labor committee in January 2007, reported favorably with a substitute amendment within two months, placed on the Senate calendar — and it ultimately passed both chambers and was signed by President Bush in May 2008 as Public Law 110-233.

narrative.text: Sen. Olympia Snowe introduced the bill on January 22, 2007 with a bipartisan list of original cosponsors including Edward Kennedy, Michael Enzi, Hillary Clinton, Barack Obama, John McCain-era Republicans John Ensign-era figures such as Wayne Allard, Ben Nelson collaborators, and Senators Hatch, Gregg, Collins, Murkowski, Hagel, Warner, and Specter.
The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on January 31, 2007.

Chairman Kennedy reported the bill to the Senate on March 29, 2007, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 97, with the written committee report filed April 10, 2007.
The bill became law: Public Law 110-233, signed by President George W. Bush in May 2008.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill passed and became law, the gain went to ordinary people carrying genetic risk, who can now be tested and seek care without the fear of losing their health coverage or their job. Genetic testing and genomics companies also gained, since fear of discrimination had been suppressing demand for their tests. Insurers and employers lost the option they would have preferred to keep: using genetic information in pricing and hiring.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People at genetic risk; testing firms

industries.note: The bill strips insurers of the ability to deny coverage, set premiums, or require genetic tests based on genetic information, and bars them from buying genetic data for underwriting. Insurers had treated genetic risk as a reason to charge more or refuse coverage; shifting that risk back onto them is precisely what the public gained. Violations carry penalties of $100 per day per affected person, with higher minimums.

Employers lose the option of genetic screening in hiring and employment decisions and take on recordkeeping duties — genetic information must be segregated in confidential medical files. The compliance cost is modest, but the practice the bill removes was discrimination against workers and applicants.

Congress's own findings noted that fear of discrimination was keeping people from taking advantage of genetic testing and new therapies; removing that fear grows the market for tests, counseling, and genomics services. The industry's gain here tracks the public's, since people can use the tests without the result being used against them in health coverage or work.
